name: corn fried zucchini slices
instructions:
Thin zucchini rounds double-dredged (milk-and-egg wash, then masa harina dry mix) and pan-fried in high-heat vegetable oil until the corn crust is crisp and golden. Corn fried in the sense of masa-crusted, not cornmeal-crusted (masa harina specifically — see notes).

=== INGREDIENTS ===

- zucchini
- vegetable oil (for frying — high heat)
- masa harina
- salt and black pepper
- milk
- 1 egg

=== PROCEDURE ===

1. SLICE THE ZUCCHINI THIN: use a mandolin to get uniformly thin slices. Uniform thinness matters — thicker slices don't cook through in the short frying time, thinner slices crisp up more evenly.
2. WET DREDGE: in a bowl, whisk together the milk and egg. Toss the zucchini slices in this mixture until coated.
3. DRY DREDGE: in a separate bowl, combine the masa harina with salt and pepper. Toss the wet zucchini slices in the masa harina mix until each slice is coated.
4. HIGH-HEAT FRY: heat vegetable oil in a large skillet or griddle over high heat until shimmering. Add the coated slices in a single layer (don't crowd). Fry until the corn crust is crisp and golden on both sides — flip once.
5. Drain briefly on paper towels. Serve hot.

=== SKILLET CHOICE ===

Don't use an iron skillet unless it's a large griddle that can accommodate many slices at once. See notes on why.
notes:
=== MASA HARINA IS THE CRUST, NOT CORNMEAL ===

Specifically masa harina (nixtamalized corn flour used for tortillas and tamales), not cornmeal. The masa gives a finer, more integrated corn crust that adheres to the wet zucchini slices — cornmeal is coarser and reads gritty in this format.

=== SKIP THE IRON SKILLET UNLESS IT'S A LARGE GRIDDLE ===

Iron skillets are usually the wrong pan for this recipe. The main problem: iron skillets tend to be small, and small pans mean you're cooking in batches. Between batches, the masa harina residue that fell off the slices during the previous fry sits in the hot oil and burns — quickly. By the time you're loading the second batch, the pan smells like burnt masa.

EXCEPTION — A LARGE IRON GRIDDLE: if you have a big flat iron griddle that can fit many slices at once (single-batch or close to it), iron is fine. The problem isn't iron per se — it's the batch-and-wait cycle that makes the caked masa burn between rounds. A big surface that lets you fry everything at once sidesteps the issue.

=== TOP FAILURE MODE — CAKED-ON MASA BURNING BETWEEN ROUNDS ===

The #1 failure mode for this recipe: masa harina flakes off the slices during frying and cakes onto the pan surface. When you load the next round, those cake bits burn in the hot oil, adding a bitter burnt-corn note to the fresh slices and eventually smoking out the kitchen.

Mitigation:
- Use a big pan (see skillet note above) so you can fry in fewer batches (ideally one).
- Wipe the pan between batches with a paper towel (carefully — the pan is hot) to remove the loose masa before adding the next round.
- Keep the oil clean by scooping out visible burnt-masa bits with a slotted spoon between slices if you see them accumulating.

=== NO CHEESE — RUINS IT ===

Don't add cheese to these. Not shredded on top before/after frying, not gratin-baked with cheese as a finish, not stirred into the masa dredge. Any cheese addition ruins the recipe. Two reasons:

- THE MASA HARINA IS ENOUGH SAVORY: the corn crust already carries the savory register the dish needs. Adding cheese on top piles savory on savory in a way that reads redundant and heavy rather than complementary.
- THE SLICES ARE DELICATE AT THE END: they're crisp-crusted zucchini rounds, not a sturdy substrate that can carry a cheese layer. Going for a gratin (melting cheese on top under a broiler) collapses the crust and turns the delicate texture into something soggy and heavy. The whole point of the recipe is the crisp-corn-crust-on-mild-zucchini balance; cheese destroys both sides of that.

Save cheese for other zucchini preparations (parmigiana-style, stuffed, etc.) where the format actually welcomes it. This one is deliberately clean.

=== SERVE HOT — DOESN'T RECOVER FROM COOLING ===

These are best eaten immediately off the pan. The masa crust softens as it cools, and reheating them under a broiler or oven gets you dry-and-limp rather than restored-and-crisp. Plan the timing.
